purpose: Third deep-expansion pass covering the next eight adjacent records with populated historical, organizational, textual, geographic, relational and evidence layers.

identity.name: Ordo Templi Orientis
identity.geographic_core: German-speaking Europe, Britain, North America and later international branches

foundational_figures: Heinrich Tränker and other early collaborators
formation.historical_field: Masonic and Rosicrucian revival, Theosophy, European occultism and Lebensreform milieus
formation.masonic_context: Early OTO developed from Masonic-derived rites; its claims of Masonic regularity and succession were contested.
formation.crowley_period: Aleister Crowley became central after his contact with Reuss and reorganized OTO around Thelema.

worldview.framework: Syncretic esotericism combining initiatory symbolism, Thelema, Hermetic and Masonic forms and ritual magic.
worldview.thelemic_layer: Under Crowley, OTO became a principal organizational vehicle for Thelema.
worldview.initiation: Degrees frame progressive participation in the order's esoteric system.

practice.gnostic_mass: The Gnostic Mass became a major public-facing ritual expression of Thelemic OTO practice.
practice.study: Members encounter ritual, philosophical and magical instruction appropriate to degree.
practice.integrity: Sexual-magic material is recorded historically and non-operationally.

texts.textual_status: Organizational and initiatory corpus rather than one closed scripture.

people.succession: Post-Reuss and post-Crowley leadership generated competing claims and later lineages.

organization.structure: Graded initiatory order with lodges, camps and affiliated bodies.
organization.governance: Supreme leadership changed over time; succession is historically complex.
organization.internationality: Branches developed in Europe, North America and elsewhere.

geography.evidence: Charters, correspondence, membership records and lodge histories.

society.culture: Important twentieth-century carrier of Crowleyan Thelema and Western occultism.
society.public_private: Much activity is initiatory/private while selected rituals and publications are public.

evidence.confidence: high for organizational history, major figures and documents; lower for disputed early lineage and succession

sources.title: The Unknown God: W. T. Smith and the Thelemites

identity.name: Anthroposophy
identity.geographic_core: Central Europe, Switzerland and global networks

formation.precursor: Steiner emerged from the German Theosophical milieu and led its German Section before breaking with the Society.
formation.formation: Anthroposophy developed as Steiner's distinct spiritual-scientific movement in the early twentieth century.
formation.institutionalization: The Anthroposophical Society and Goetheanum became principal centers.

worldview.core: Spiritual knowledge is presented as a disciplined investigation of human beings, nature and cosmic evolution.
worldview.human_model: Steiner described physical, soul and spiritual dimensions and stages of consciousness.
worldview.christology: Christ has a central role in Steiner's esoteric interpretation of human and cosmic evolution.
worldview.reincarnation: Reincarnation and karma are major doctrines.

practice.meditation: Meditative exercises for attention and spiritual perception.
practice.education: Waldorf education applies selected anthroposophical developmental ideas.
practice.agriculture: Steiner's 1924 Agriculture Course became the basis of biodynamic agriculture.
practice.arts: Eurythmy, architecture, visual arts and speech work developed in the movement.

texts.status: Books and extensive lecture corpus form the principal textual record.
texts.interpretation: Texts combine philosophy, esoteric revelation, biography and practical institutional guidance.

geography.global: Anthroposophical institutions developed across Europe and globally.

society.education: Waldorf schools became its most visible institutional application.
society.medicine: Anthroposophical medicine is a distinct historical current; empirical claims require independent evaluation.

evidence.confidence: high for biography, organizations, publications and institutional history

sources.title: Eco-Alchemy: Anthroposophy and the History and Future of Environmentalism

evidence.integrity: Institutional history is not treated as validation of supernatural or medical claims.

formation.foundation: LaVey established the Church of Satan in San Francisco in 1966.
formation.historical_field: 1960s counterculture, secularization, Western occult revival and literary Satanic symbolism.

worldview.theology: LaVeyan Satanism is generally described as non-theistic or atheistic.
worldview.satan_symbol: Satan functions primarily as a symbol of individualism, self-assertion, natural desire and opposition to conventional morality.
worldview.ethics: Personal responsibility, self-preservation and individual liberty are emphasized.
worldview.anti_religion: Critiques conventional Christian morality and perceived religious repression.

practice.ritual: Ritual is framed largely as psychodrama and symbolic magic rather than literal Satan worship.
practice.organization: Formal titles, clergy structures and membership arrangements have existed and changed over time.

organization.form: Religious organization with clergy/titular structures and affiliated activity.
organization.schism: Michael Aquino and others departed in 1975 and formed the Temple of Set.
organization.identity_boundary: Distinct from The Satanic Temple and theistic Satanisms.

geography.expansion: National and international reach through books, media and correspondence.

society.counterculture: Prominent countercultural religion of the late 1960s and 1970s.
society.media: Media attention strongly shaped public perceptions.
society.moral_panic: Later Satanic Panic claims must be separated from documented organizational history.

evidence.confidence: high for founding, texts and organizational history

sources.title: Children of Lucifer: The Origins of Modern Religious Satanism
The Age of Satanism: Anton LaVey and the Church of Satan

evidence.integrity: Self-identification, scholarship and hostile accusations remain separate.

formation.emergence: The movement emerged in the early 2010s in the United States through public campaigns and media activity.
formation.historical_field: Secularism, religious pluralism, church-state law, internet culture and modern Satanic identity.
formation.distinction: Organizationally and doctrinally distinct from the Church of Satan.

worldview.theology: Generally non-theistic and symbolic rather than belief in a literal Satan.
worldview.ethical_framework: The Seven Fundamental Tenets emphasize compassion, reason, bodily autonomy, personal freedom and proportional justice.
worldview.satan_symbol: Satan is presented as a symbol of rebellion against arbitrary authority and defense of autonomy.

practice.rituals: Ceremonies and rituals can function as religious or symbolic expression.
practice.activism: Religious-liberty, bodily-autonomy and church-state campaigns are central.
practice.community: Chapters and online networks provide community structures.

texts.interpretive_source: Greaves's 2017 comparison with the Church of Satan is a primary self-representational source.

organization.form: Contemporary religious organization with chapters, membership structures and public advocacy.
organization.public_strategy: Legal and media campaigns test practical religious-pluralism principles.

society.law: Religious-liberty disputes are important to public activity.
society.pluralism: Useful case study of minority religion operating through equal-treatment principles.

evidence.confidence: high for public activity, texts and campaigns

sources.title: Lucien Greaves, 'Church of Satan vs. Satanic Temple'

evidence.integrity: Self-description is separated from external political characterization.

identity.name: Temple of Set
identity.geographic_core: United States with international initiatory network

formation.origin: Formed in 1975 following Aquino's break with the Church of Satan.
formation.historical_field: Post-LaVeyan Satanism, Western esotericism and Egyptian religious symbolism.
formation.doctrinal_shift: Aquino developed a Set-centered theology distinct from LaVeyan symbolic Satanism.

worldview.central_principle: Set is understood as a metaphysical and initiatory principle associated with individual consciousness and self-becoming.
worldview.xeper: Xeper is a central Setian concept of becoming or self-development.
worldview.individuality: The tradition emphasizes development of the individual self.
worldview.egyptian_connection: Modern Setian theology invokes Set but is not treated as unchanged ancient Egyptian religion.

practice.initiation: Graded initiatory work and individual study.
practice.magic: Ritual and magical practices are framed as transformative work.
practice.pylons: Pylons function as organizational and initiatory groupings.

central: The Book of Coming Forth by Night
Temple of Set writings and degree material
texts.status: Primary evidence for Setian self-understanding; revelation claims are not independent empirical proof.

organization.structure: Priesthood, Council of Nine, pylons and graded initiatory degrees.
organization.membership: Selective initiatory participation rather than mass membership.

geography.network: International membership developed through local and correspondence structures.

society.classification: Studied variously as Satanism, post-Satanism or Left-Hand Path religion.
society.reception: Important example of modern reinterpretation of an ancient deity without assuming institutional continuity.

evidence.confidence: high for 1975 formation, Aquino's role and surviving texts

sources.title: Michael Aquino, The Book of Coming Forth by Night (1975)
Satanism: A Reader, chapter on Michael Aquino

evidence.integrity: Ancient Set and modern Setian religion are connected by symbolic reference, not assumed continuity.

identity.name: Order of Nine Angles
identity.geographic_core: United Kingdom and transnational online networks
identity.attributed_founder: Associated with the pseudonym Anton Long; origins and authorship are contested.

formation.historical_field: British occult milieu, Satanism, National Socialist and radical political esotericism.
formation.origin_claims: Claims of ancient lineage are not independently established historical fact.
formation.development: The movement circulated through texts, small cells and later online dissemination.

worldview.framework: The Sinister Tradition combines occult self-transformation, radical transgression and political-esoteric themes.
worldview.political_overlap: Scholarship documents intersections involving National Socialist and radical political milieus.
worldview.integrity: Extremist dimensions are documented as research subjects, not endorsed.

practice.structure: Texts describe initiatory stages, but operational instructions for harmful or extremist activity are intentionally not reproduced.
practice.textual_dissemination: The movement relies heavily on internally circulated manuals and mythic-historical narratives.

texts.status: Primary evidence for self-description; texts do not prove claimed ancient lineage.

organization.form: Loose occult network with cells, pseudonymous authorship and decentralized dissemination.
organization.centralization: No transparent conventional hierarchy is established.
organization.membership: Reliable membership estimates are difficult because of deliberate opacity.

society.extremism: Important to research on intersections between occultism and extremist politics.
society.documented_associations: Academic work documents extremist political associations involving figures connected with the movement.
society.media: Internet dissemination expanded access to ONA material.

documented_intersections: radical Islamist milieus involving associated figures

evidence.confidence: high for existence of ONA texts and ideological corpus; moderate for early organizational history

sources.title: The Order of the Nine Angles, The Black Book of Satan (1984)
Secret Identities in the Sinister Tradition

evidence.integrity: No recruitment, romanticization or operationalization of extremist material.

identity.name: Process Church of the Final Judgment
identity.category: new religious movement / apocalyptic esoteric religion
identity.geographic_core: United Kingdom and United States, especially California

formation.origin: The movement developed from the de Grimstons' earlier Scientology-linked background before becoming an independent religious movement.
formation.historical_field: 1960s counterculture, occult revival, apocalyptic Christianity and Satanic symbolism.
formation.expansion: Centers and communities were established in several locations, especially in the United States.

worldview.core_theology: The Process Church developed a distinctive theology presenting apparently opposed divine figures within a larger cosmic unity.
worldview.apocalypse: Apocalyptic transformation and reconciliation of opposites were major themes.

practice.community: Members participated in communal religious life and centers.
practice.worship: Ritual and devotional practices drew on Christian and Satanic imagery.
practice.publications: Magazines and pamphlets were important vehicles of doctrine and recruitment.

texts.status: Published texts provide direct evidence for theology and public self-presentation.

people.leadership: The de Grimstons were central to doctrinal development.

organization.form: Communal religious movement with centers in several countries.
organization.transformation: The organization underwent substantial changes during the 1970s rather than continuing unchanged.

major_centers: Los Angeles and other California locations

society.counterculture: Associated with 1960s and 1970s alternative religion and counterculture.
society.conspiracy: Later conspiracy narratives exaggerated links to unrelated criminal events and must not replace documentary evidence.
society.media: Its unusual theology attracted substantial media attention.

evidence.confidence: high for existence, founders, publications and major theology

sources.title: The Process Church of the Final Judgement, 'The Gods on War' and 'The Gods and Their People'

evidence.integrity: Documented history remains separate from later conspiracy narratives.

identity.name: Militant Anti-Religious / State-Attempted Secularization Movements
identity.period: late 18th–20th centuries, with major revolutionary and state campaigns in the 20th century
identity.geographic_core: France, Soviet Union and other states pursuing aggressive secularization
languages: and local languages of affected states

formation.historical_field: Enlightenment criticism of clerical power, materialism, revolutionary politics, Marxism-Leninism and state-building.
important_cases: Cultural Revolution-era attacks on religious institutions
formation.distinction: Anti-religion, atheism, secularism and anti-clericalism are distinct categories and must not be collapsed.

worldview.problem: Religion could be interpreted by some movements as an obstacle to revolutionary transformation, scientific education or political modernization.
worldview.goal: Goals ranged from limiting clerical power and separating church from state to attempting to eliminate religious institutions or belief.
worldview.afterlife: Materialist currents generally rejected supernatural afterlife claims, but revolutionary states could replace religious structures with civic rituals and ideological education.
worldview.ethics: Ethical systems varied: utilitarian, republican, socialist, Marxist and humanist forms all occurred.

state_campaigns: closure or repurposing of religious buildings
restrictions on clergy and religious associations
replacement_rituals: Revolutionary Cults of Reason and Supreme Being in France
practice.integrity: These were political and social programs, not one coherent religion with a universal ritual system.

texts.textual_status: Heterogeneous ideological and administrative corpus rather than one canon.

people.state_actors: Different revolutionary governments and party organizations implemented anti-religious programs in different ways.
people.critics: Religious leaders, believers and later historians documented resistance, accommodation and consequences.

organization.membership_model: Political parties, civic associations, propaganda leagues and state institutions rather than a single religious membership body.
organization.offices: Government ministries, party committees and propaganda organizations often administered campaigns.
organization.recruitment: Education and political mobilization were major recruitment mechanisms.
organization.public_or_private: Primarily public and state-directed, though individual unbelief remained distinct from state policy.

geography.sites: Former churches, monasteries, museums, archives and propaganda institutions preserve evidence of changing state-religion relations.

society.state_relation: The defining feature was an attempt to restructure the legal and institutional relationship between state and religion.
society.law: Laws could nationalize property, restrict worship, remove religious education or change recognition of religious institutions.
society.politics: Anti-religious policy was often embedded in wider revolutionary or authoritarian projects.
society.education: Schools became important sites of secular or atheist education.
society.media: Newspapers, posters, books, radio and public lectures were used for propaganda.
society.resistance: Believers and local officials sometimes resisted, adapted or selectively implemented state directives.

relationships.internal_variation: French republican anticlericalism, Soviet militant atheism and Chinese Cultural Revolution policies must be studied as separate cases.

interpretation.community_self_description: Varied by movement and period; some described their goal as emancipation from clerical domination rather than elimination of personal religion.
interpretation.scholarly_description: Best treated as a family of political and secularizing projects rather than a single anti-religion.
interpretation.outsider_polemics: Both anti-religious and religious polemics can exaggerate uniformity or intentionality.
interpretation.modern_reconstruction: Comparative analysis should preserve country, regime and time period.

evidence.confidence: high for documented legislation, organizations and campaigns; variable for motives and effects at local level

sources.title: The Philosophes and Religion: Intellectual Origins of the Dechristianization Movement in the French Revolution
The French Revolution and religion to 1794
Commissars in Red Cassocks: Former Priests in the League of the Militant Godless
Fear no evil: schools and religion in Soviet Russia, 1917–1941

contested: relative weight of Enlightenment ideas versus wartime and political motives in French dechristianization
local variation in Soviet anti-religious implementation
comparability of different state secularization projects

integrity.historical_fact_vs_later_legend: Use legislation, archival records and contemporary publications.
integrity.self_description_vs_external_label: Distinguish atheism, secularism, anti-clericalism and anti-religion.
integrity.ancient_cult_vs_modern_revival: Not applicable; this is a modern political family.
integrity.symbolic_similarity_vs_historical_influe: Do not infer ideological influence from generic secular language alone.
integrity.secret_claim_vs_documented_evidence: State campaigns should be reconstructed from documentary evidence, not conspiracy narratives.

sources_note: The third expansion uses academic research and primary institutional materials where available; disputed theological, lineage and political claims are explicitly separated from historical evidence.
integrity: No placeholders are used. The eight records are distinct canonical expansions; Theosophical Society is intentionally not duplicated here because it is already expanded in deep-expansions-2.json.
